title: Helping helps the helper
hook: volunteering is linked to better wellbeing in many studies, though cause and effect are hard to prove

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maimonides' ladder and the gift nobody sees. Your line was unseen. Did you manage not to tell anyone? Day one hundred forty.

Think of the last time you really helped someone. Carried a stroller up the subway stairs. Sat with a friend through a hard night. Spent a Saturday at a food bank. Now think about how you felt walking away. For a lot of people, the honest answer is: better. Lighter. Sometimes better than the person they helped. That feels almost like cheating, as if service should cost something. But researchers have been measuring it for decades, and the pattern keeps showing up. Today's practice is helping helps the helper.
screen: `CARRYING THE STROLLER.` → `WALKING AWAY LIGHTER.` → `HELPING HELPS THE HELPER.`

segments.voice: In the late nineteen eighties, a writer named Allan Luks surveyed thousands of volunteers. Many described the same thing: a warm rush while helping, followed by a longer calm. He called it the helper's high, and the name stuck. Then the lab got involved. In a 2008 study, researchers handed people envelopes of cash, five or twenty dollars, and told some to spend it on themselves and others to spend it on someone else by evening. The ones who spent it on others were happier at the end of the day. The amount didn't seem to matter much. Then the long studies. Across many countries, people who volunteer tend to report better wellbeing, and in some studies of older adults, volunteers even lived longer. Now the honest part, the part that's easy to skip. Most of this research finds a link, not a proof. Healthier, happier people may simply be more likely to volunteer in the first place. Untangling cause and effect is hard, and good scientists say so. So nobody can promise that helping will fix your mood. What the evidence does allow is this: helping is at least as good for many helpers as we'd hope, and often better. And traditions have said something like it for a long time, each in its own way. But here's the catch. If you help only to feel good, you'll start watching yourself instead of the person. The good feeling works best as a surprise, not a goal. So notice it when it comes. It comes back.
screen: `THE HELPER'S HIGH.` · `FIVE DOLLARS FOR SOMEONE ELSE.` · `A LINK, NOT A PROOF.` · `A SURPRISE, NOT A GOAL.` · then, large: `IT COMES BACK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice how you feel after helping. Settle, and breathe. Bring back a time you helped someone, recently or long ago. Replay the moment right after. Where in your body did you feel it? The chest, the face, the shoulders? Was it warmth, relief, tiredness, or nothing much? All of it is information. Just notice, without grading it. The bell holds the time.
Helping helps the helper. Many studies link helping others with the helper's own wellbeing, even if cause and effect are hard to prove. Today's word.
Your line: it comes back. Today, after you help someone, even in a tiny way, pause for one breath and notice how you feel. Day one hundred forty.

howItsDone: Many volunteers describe a warm lift after helping, and wellbeing researchers study it through surveys, experiments with small gifts, and long-term studies of people who volunteer.
